source: Chollet et al. (2026) ARC Prize 2025: Technical Report
finding: Top Kaggle scores on ARC-AGI-2 private set came from test-time training, synthetic data and ensembles, not from length-based selection. No Kaggle winner is described as using MDL or code length.
numbers: 1,455 teams, 15,154 entries. Private ARC-AGI-2: NVARC 24.03% ($0.20/task), ARChitects 16.53%, MindsAI 12.64%, Lonnie 6.67%, Barbadillo 6.53%. ARChitects use a masked-diffusion LM with 'perspective-based scoring'. 90 papers submitted.
limits: Report is a short summary; solution internals are in the teams' own write-ups, which were not opened. Absence of mention is not proof of absence of use.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 5 for the Kaggle track: the best 2025 systems select by model likelihood across augmented views (a code-length-like score) but none is a stated MDL selector. Our selector idea is untested at this scale.

source: Chollet et al. (2026) ARC Prize 2025: Technical Report (paper awards section)
finding: CompressARC (3rd paper award) is the only MDL system among the winners. Its ARC-AGI-2 score is low. TRM (1st paper award) and SOAR (2nd) are the other program or refinement systems.
numbers: CompressARC 20% ARC-AGI-1 eval (up to 34% quoted for train), 4% ARC-AGI-2, 76K parameters, about 20 min on one RTX 4070 per puzzle. TRM 45% ARC-AGI-1, 8% ARC-AGI-2 with 7M parameters. SOAR: up to +52% relative gain on ARC-AGI-1.
quote: CompressARC ... achieves 20-34% on ARC-AGI-1 and 4% on ARC-AGI-2 without any pretraining or external data.
limits: ARC-AGI-2 figure for CompressARC is the organisers' statement; the CompressARC paper itself (opened earlier) is the source for ARC-AGI-1.
agent_relevance: Pure MDL by gradient descent drops from 20% to 4% on the harder set, the same collapse seen for DSL search (K14).

source: Chollet et al. (2026) ARC Prize 2025: Technical Report (refinement loops)
finding: Report names the refinement loop as the 2025 theme. A commercial reasoning chain is read as a natural-language program that is refined. Reasoning token count rises with higher thinking modes, even when not needed.
numbers: Task 4cd1b7b2: Gemini 3 Pro 96 reasoning tokens, Gemini 3 Deep Think 138,000 tokens. Poetiq harness on Gemini 3 Pro: ARC-AGI-2 31% at $0.81/task to 54% at $31/task; similar gain on Claude Opus 4.5 at about $60/task (as reported by Poetiq).
quote: Gemini 3 Pro used 96 reasoning tokens to solve this task, whereas Gemini 3 Deep Think employed 138,000 tokens.
limits: One task as example. No correlation between shorter trace and correctness is reported; the report says more tokens go with more refinement, not that shorter or longer is right. Poetiq figures are self-reported and only verified for the Gemini run.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: no study found that links shorter reasoning traces to correct answers on ARC-AGI-2. The only public datum is that thinking effort scales cost, not that length signals truth.

source: Pourcel, Colas, Oudeyer (2025) Self-Improving Language Models for Evolutionary Program Synthesis (SOAR)
finding: SOAR picks final outputs by weighted vote over test outputs of programs sampled and refined by an LLM. Weight is the program's training-example accuracy, not its length. Voting leaves a gap to the oracle.
numbers: 6k candidate programs per task (3k sampled, 3k refined). Weight = count + 1000 x mean train accuracy. Average gap between majority voting and oracle (any candidate correct): 9.5 points across models. Pooling the search traces of five model sizes beat each single model. Final public-test score 52%.
quote: majority voting is not an ideal aggregation strategy
limits: Selection is by example accuracy plus vote; no length term and no ablation of one. Oracle gap is on ARC-AGI-1 public tasks with open models.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: this is the closest published selector among fitting LLM programs, and it ignores length. A length tie-break on top of train accuracy is untested.

source: Pourcel, Colas, Oudeyer (2025) SOAR, appendix F
finding: LLM programs sometimes fit the examples by hard-coding: they compute grid size, then map it to copied training outputs. These fit all examples and skew the vote.
numbers: Detected by checking whether any training output appears as a literal in the code; the authors say this check removes them. No rate is reported.
limits: Qualitative; no count of how often it happens.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: a concrete, cheap guard against fit-but-wrong. Reject any program that contains its training outputs, then prefer the shorter of what remains.

source: Moghe and Chin (2026) Cost-Effective Agent Harnesses for Abstract Reasoning on ARC-AGI-1
finding: With DeepSeek V3.2 (non-thinking, no ARC training), choosing among 5 candidate programs by training-pair accuracy recovers about 95% of the best possible. The loss is mostly tasks where no candidate is right.
numbers: Pipeline: 57.50% pass@2 at $0.25/task (one-shot 15.50%, structured CoT 30.00%). Unbiased pass@1 46.40% vs pass@2 with train-score selection 57.50%. Orchestrator: 67.25% pass@2 at $0.62/task, unbiased pass@1 56.21%, selection again 95% of ceiling. Lift orchestrator minus pipeline +9.75 pp (paired bootstrap CI +6.50 to +13.25). Correct-count per task is bimodal.
quote: selection via training-pair accuracy captures 95% of the candidate ceiling
limits: Preprint, one model, ARC-AGI-1 public eval (400 tasks), M=5 only; 95% is relative to a pass@M ceiling that is itself limited at M=5. Selection used train exact match plus dedup by test grid, not length.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 and 3: once a candidate fits all examples, picking among fitters is rarely the bottleneck here. An MDL selector can add little on this benchmark with M=5. Effort belongs in generation breadth.

source: Moghe and Chin (2026) Cost-Effective Agent Harnesses (selection and failure modes)
finding: Several independent definers often converge on the same wrong rule. Counting convergent outputs as one vote (dedup by test prediction) stops them from crowding out a lone correct program.
numbers: Worked case in the appendix: four convergent wrong definers would have filled pass@2; dedup keeps the dissenter. Tie on training score broken by agent index.
quote: definers frequently converge on the same wrong rule
limits: Mechanism shown by worked examples; no numeric ablation with and without dedup was found in the parts read.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: plain majority vote among fitting programs can be worse than a diversity-aware pick. Any MDL-versus-vote test should include a dedup arm.

source: Land (2026) Modality-Driven Search with Holistic Trace Judging for ARC-AGI-2
finding: With 8 to 29 candidates from text, image and code channels, a long-context judge that reads all traces beats majority vote by 7 solved instances on the public ARC-AGI-2 set. All 7 were cases where the right answer was a minority.
numbers: Semi-private 72.9% at $38.99/task; public eval 76.1% at $19.69/task (GPT-5.2 Pro alone 54.2%, Gemini 3 Pro 54.0%). 167 public instances: solved 128 (76.65%); pool had a correct output in 144 (86.23%). Unsolved 39 = 22 no correct candidate (13.17%), 17 correct but not picked (10.18%); the failure section counts 21 generation failures, 17 selection failures and 1 early-stop case.
quote: the correct solution to an unsolved task is often not the modal answer
limits: Single author, not peer-reviewed. Prompts and mix tuned on the same public sets. Judge is the same model family as the generators. Does not test length-based selection.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 and 5: on ARC-AGI-2 the modal answer is often wrong, so simplicity or consensus selectors may fail where the right rule is rare. Selection loss (10%) is about as large as generation loss (13%).

source: Land (2026) Modality-Driven Search (judge variants and groupthink case)
finding: A judge that scores 'logical consistency' failed because a candidate can be logical yet overfit the training pairs. A consistency judge rewarded the wrong majority. Task dfadab01:1 shows the pattern.
numbers: dfadab01:1: 12 candidates agree on one wrong output, 8 on a second wrong output, 1 candidate is correct and was picked by the judges. Three homogeneous GPT-5.2 judges beat a mixed Opus, Gemini, GPT-5.2 panel.
quote: a candidate can be 'logical' yet overfit to training pairs
limits: Qualitative; no table giving the accuracy of the logic and consistency judges.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: names fit-but-wrong as a real failure for ARC-AGI-2 LLM programs; shows that agreement between samples is not evidence of truth. The simplicity check must not be replaced by agreement.

source: Barber, Young, Coombe, Browne (2025) Solomonoff-Inspired Hypothesis Ranking with LLMs
finding: Closest direct test of length-weighted selection for LLM hypotheses. GPT-4 writes 6 or 20 hypotheses per Mini-ARC task. Score = (1 - normalised token length) x cell accuracy on training grids. Compared with Bayesian model averaging (accuracy only, uniform prior).
numbers: Three tasks only. Task A: Solomonoff-weighted mixture 64% vs BMA 48% cell accuracy (6 hypotheses). Task B: both 100%. Task C with 20 noisy hypotheses: Solomonoff 60% vs BMA 64%.
limits: Anecdote-scale (3 tasks, 5x5 grids, one run). Length proxy is hypothesis text tokens, not program length. Hypotheses are object-level natural language. Authors say good candidates need prompt engineering.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 and 6: only published length-versus-fit comparison with an LLM on ARC-like tasks, and it is a wash (win, tie, loss). Not enough to accept or reject a length prior.

source: Zhu (2026) Think Through a Bottleneck: Hourglass Reasoning for Rigorous Induction
finding: Prompt-only compression of the examples into a short symbolic schema and rule, passed between isolated contexts, lifts ARC-AGI-2 on frozen LLMs over a self-refine baseline.
numbers: ARC-AGI-2 public 120 tasks, pass@1 / pass@5: GPT-5.5 Self-Refine 51.9 / 62.8 vs Hourglass 60.6 / 76.8 (+8.7 / +14.0); Gemini 3.1 Pro 54.4 / 76.9 vs 62.4 / 86.7 (+8.0 / +9.8). Competition mode: 87.8% pass@2 at about $3.98/task; oracle ceiling 91.4 to 95.4%.
quote: information can only pass between them as a compressed symbolic state
limits: Preprint, one author, models later than our other sources. 'Compression' here is a rule plus schema, not a measured code length; no arm picks by shortest description. pass@5 uses early stopping (authors flag optimistic bias).
agent_relevance: Gap 6: a prompt-only agent that compresses examples to a rule first (S2) then checks by execution does measurably better. This supports the scaffold idea, though not the MDL scoring itself.

finding: The gain comes from isolating stages, not from rule wording. Asking for the same structured rule inside one context did worse than plain self-refine. A weak first induction cannot be repaired.
numbers: Pass@1 / pass@5. Full 60.6/76.8 (GPT-5.5), 62.4/86.7 (Gemini). Struct-SR 41.5/59.9 and 31.6/62.8, below SR baseline. Weak-Init 40.1/61.4 and 54.3/74.6. Plain 59.9/79.3 and 70.1/87.5. Code-Only 58.1/74.7 and 72.8/79.9.
quote: Such patches force support examples to pass but fail on out-of-distribution queries
limits: Single author, one benchmark for this ablation. Prompt includes an 'anti-patching' rule against if color == 3 branches, never ablated alone.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 and 6: 'state the rule first' is not enough without context isolation. Patchwork if-else code is named as the way programs fit examples yet fail on the query. Put the rule check in a fresh context.

source: Vahdati et al. (2026) The ARC of Progress towards AGI: A Living Survey
finding: Survey of 82 ARC approaches places MADIL on the 2022-2025 timeline and cites CompressARC as 'compression as intelligence'. It reports no independent re-run, extension or fork of MADIL.
numbers: Search of the PDF text for MADIL found: one entry in the performance-over-time figure, one reference (Ferre 2025), no results table of its own. Survey states a 2.5 to 3 times degradation from ARC-AGI-1 to ARC-AGI-2 across approaches.
limits: Absence in a survey is weak evidence. The survey is a secondary source and the figure is hard to read in text form.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: still no replication found. Treat MADIL numbers as one-author results.

source: Semantic Scholar citation listing for CompressARC (arXiv 2512.06104), fetched this session
finding: Four citing papers found for CompressARC: a neural-cellular-automata ARC paper, a discrete-diffusion composition paper, an agentic-framework survey, and an ARC survey. None is a re-run of CompressARC.
numbers: Citing ids: 2506.15746, 2607.11758, 2604.16646, one survey with no arXiv id. The citation lookup for MADIL (2505.01081) returned HTTP 429 and OpenAlex was out of budget, so MADIL's citers were not retrieved.
limits: Index is incomplete and lags. For MADIL the check failed, so it cannot be called empty.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: no independent CompressARC replication found; MADIL citer list not obtained.

source: Ferre (2025) MADIL, discussion and Definitions 2 (re-read for priors)
finding: MADIL's code lengths come from hand-chosen value distributions: uniform over intervals for integers and motif lists, and a split of background colours (black likely) from object colours (black unlikely). The author lists learning primitives as an open problem and no flat-prior ablation is reported.
numbers: No table varies the prior. Author lists limits: combinatorial decompositions, input and output models learned separately, no conditionals, hard sequence matching, no constraints between parts.
limits: Based on a read of the PDF text for priors and future-work sections; a negative finding ('no ablation') depends on that text being complete.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 stays open: no evidence either way on whether a flat or learned prior would match hand-set code lengths. The agent should state its coding scheme and not assume the scheme is neutral.

source: LeGris, Vong, Lake, Gureckis (2024) H-ARC, discussion section (re-read)
finding: H-ARC collected written solution descriptions and action traces but does not analyse description length against solve rate. It only suggests that evaluation-set programs may be longer than training-set ones as one reason for lower human accuracy.
numbers: Human accuracy 76.2% train vs 64.2% eval (3 attempts). Descriptions collected after first attempt and after later correct or final attempts.
limits: The authors write 'We hope' the descriptions will help; no number is given. Johnson et al. 2021 (b = -0.17, 40 tasks) remains the only measured link.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 stays open: the data exist but no one in the sources found has run the length-versus-difficulty analysis on H-ARC.

source: Ouellette (2025) Out-of-Distribution Generalization in the ARC-AGI Domain: Execution-Guided Neural Program Synthesis vs Test-Time Fine-Tuning
finding: Controlled compositional test: a model that builds programs step by step with execution feedback composes novel solutions better than test-time fine-tuning, which seems to mainly bring out knowledge already in the model.
numbers: Reported figure for the execution-guided GridCoder2 variant: solves 83.33% of the theoretically solvable ARC-AGI-2 training tasks (1.5% of the whole set); NN-only baseline 27.78%.
limits: Small controlled setup; the 83.33% applies to a tiny solvable subset. No length-based selection.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: execution feedback in the loop (not shortest-first) is what lets a program builder take non-greedy detours; supports allowing operators that explore beyond the shortest candidate.

source: Abstract-level listings (arXiv search pages, Oct 2026): ARCANA program-synthesis framework 2607.09059; Combining LLMs and Genetic Search for ARC-AGI-2 2609.27242
finding: Two 2026 papers verify LLM-proposed programs by running them on the demonstration pairs (ARCANA) or evolve LLM-seeded programs with a genetic algorithm. Only titles and one-line gists were seen.
limits: Not opened. Cannot say whether either uses length in selection.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 and 9: candidates for follow-up reading. Not used for claims.
